title: How To Handle An Angry Parent
author: Michael Linsin
summary: This article lays out a seven-step protocol for defusing an angry parent encounter: listen without interrupting, categorize the complaint (referring policy issues to the principal while owning classroom-management issues), empathize with the parent's feelings, take responsibility regardless of actual fault, apologize, fix the specific problem, and follow up afterward to confirm resolution. Linsin frames parents as customers whose goodwill directly benefits the teacher's reputation and classroom climate, arguing that defensiveness or arguing back only damages standing with the broader parent community. He includes a practical note recommending a first-days-of-school parent information packet to prevent many complaints before they start. The piece closes by emphasizing that the teacher's composure and follow-through, not the merits of the complaint, determine the outcome.
points: A seven-step sequence - listen, categorize, empathize, take responsibility, apologize, fix it, follow up
Complaints about school-wide policy should be redirected to the principal; classroom-level complaints should be owned and explained.
Taking responsibility and apologizing quickly diffuses anger even when the teacher isn't strictly at fault.
Sending a first-days-of-school parent information packet proactively prevents many future complaints.
Treating parents as customers protects the teacher's reputation and turns anger into long-term support.
quotes: Your first step is to do nothing. Just listen. Don’t interrupt and don’t be in a hurry to jump in. Doing so will only make them angrier and more intent on making a big issue out of it.
If the complaint is in regard to your classroom management plan, homework policy, or classroom procedures, then politely explain why you do things the way you do.
Validate the parent’s feelings by telling them that you understand why they’re upset and why they feel the way they do.

Whether or not you’re directly responsible for why the parent is angry is irrelevant. Take responsibility anyway. It’s the fastest way to diffuse their anger and is the right thing to do–for them and for you.
End your conversation by reiterating that you’re going to take care of the problem. But this time be specific.
It's best to think of parents as your customers. If you take care of them, attend to their concerns, and make them happy, it benefits you and your business.

It doesn’t matter how off base you think they are, how rude they behave, or how badly you’d like to tell them to take a hike. You have the power to keep your cool, address their concerns with class, and turn their anger into enthusiastic support.
